row.overview: Mount Fairchild (6,899 ft) is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range, a glaciated subrange deep in the interior of Olympic National Park's Daniel J. Evans Wilderness. It carries the small, retreating Fairchild Glacier on its northeast flank and sits about 0.84 mi northeast of higher neighbor Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). No trail comes anywhere close to the summit — nearly all ascents are made as a side-trip during the multi-day Bailey Range Traverse rather than as a standalone climb, and the peak sees only a handful of ascents most years. First climbed in 1963 by Denny Pruitt, Dan Baker, Jack Christiansen, and Roy Etten.
row.beta: Mount Fairchild is the second-highest peak in the Bailey Range and is accessed via two primary routes: (1) the High Divide approach via Sol Duc and Mount Carrie, or (2) from the Elwha River over Mount Fitzhenry. Both routes involve significant glacier travel with crevasse hazards and require proper alpine mountaineering skills. The peak stands at the head of Fairchild Creek with the Fairchild Glacier on its east slope.
row.turnaround: Firm turnaround; retreat options are limited
row.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
row.comms: No cell service anywhere in the Bailey Range or Olympic alpine backcountry. Satellite communicator (Garmin inReach or similar) essential for emergency communication. Contact Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center at (360) 565-3100 before trip to file itinerary.
row.descent: Descend via the standard descent route, retracing the ascent when possible. Be aware of loose rock and snow bridge hazards. Maintain group cohesion on exposed sections.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large trailhead parking lot at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road; Olympic National Park entrance pass required; overnight trips need a wilderness permit reserved in advance, since none are issued at the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Turn south off US 101 onto Sol Duc Hot Springs Road (about 29 miles west of Port Angeles) and follow it, paved the whole way, past the park entrance station, the Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort and the campground to the large lot at road's end — the trailhead is at the very end, beyond the resort.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Falls
waypoints.note: Trail crosses a footbridge just below the falls; last easy, reliable water before the climb toward Appleton Pass begins in earnest.
waypoints.directions: From the end of the lot take the Sol Duc River Trail up the valley: 0.8 mi of wide, near-level old-growth tread with essentially no elevation change (1,950 to 1,980 ft), ending at the footbridge just below the falls. This is the last easy, reliable water taken straight off the trail before the climbing starts.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Sol Duc River Trail here and turn right/uphill onto the Appleton Pass Trail; elevation is a rough interpolation along the NPS-stated 2,000-5,100 ft climb.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass
waypoints.note: Broad alpine pass on the Bailey Range crest with meadows and views into the Boulder Lake basin; leave the maintained trail here to begin cross-country travel into the Bailey Range proper.

waypoints.name: The Cat Walk (Cat Peak traverse)
waypoints.note: Old, narrow, exposed use-path sidehilling the steep flanks of Cat Peak; the steepest, most exposure-prone stretch of the whole approach, worse with a full pack.

waypoints.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
waypoints.note: Small flat tent spot at the east end of the Cat Walk with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond; water needs filtering and the site is exposed to wind/weather.
waypoints.directions: Follow the sidehill path east to the far end of the Cat Walk arete, giving back roughly 200 ft. The camp is a single small flat tent spot at the east end with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond beside it — filter that water, and expect the site to be fully exposed to wind and weather.

waypoints.name: Mount Carrie ridge/glacier gain
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Bailey Range (0.84 mi SW of Fairchild's summit); per the descent beta this is where the route regains the ridge/glacier system linking to the Fairchild Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly 1,700 ft southeast from Boston Charlie's onto Mount Carrie (6,995 ft), the highest point in the Bailey Range. There is a real choice here: many parties sidehill the loose, exposed talus across Carrie's south face, but staying higher — up the ridge on Carrie's north side, over or just under the summit — avoids the worst of the sidehilling and sets up a cleaner entry onto the Fairchild Glacier. Where the crest becomes too sharp to walk, traverse up across the scree flanks. There is no reliable water on this stretch, so tank up at camp.

waypoints.name: Fairchild Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up and don crampons/axe here; follow the wind-formed ridge down-glacier toward the exit col on Ruth Peak's shoulder — crevasse hazard, especially late season when snow bridges are thin.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 300 ft northeast off Carrie's ridge onto the upper Fairchild Glacier, which starts around 6,600-6,700 ft on the Bailey crest and falls away to the northeast. Rope up and put on crampons here; an ice axe is wanted most of the season. Rather than taking the direct line, follow the wind-formed snow ridge running down the glacier — the same idea as the Hogsback on Mount Hood — which keeps you clear of the crevasses. Late season the snow bridges thin and the surface goes to bare, hard ice, so this is full crampon technique, not microspikes.

waypoints.name: Mount Fairchild
waypoints.note: Second-highest peak in the Bailey Range; short final scramble on snow and rock from the glacier saddle to the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Leave the wind ridge and take the steeper exit section up onto Fairchild's summit ridge: roughly 35-40 degrees of snow past an icy patch, the steepest ground on the route. Stay roped and in crampons through it. From the summit ridge a short scramble on snow and rock gains the 6,899 ft true summit, second-highest in the Bailey Range. There is no rappel anywhere on this climb — the only way off is to reverse the entire line, and the glacier softens through the afternoon, so set an early turnaround.

row.detailed_rack: Glacier kit for the Fairchild Glacier crossing; light gear for Class 2-3 rock
pro_tips: reserve your Olympic NP wilderness permit on Recreation.gov as soon as the summer release window opens (around mid-April) — walk-up availability for the Baileys is limited
a light glacier kit (short rope, tibloc/microtrax, a few slings) is usually sufficient for the short Fairchild/Carrie Glacier crossings rather than a full mountaineering rack
plan Fairchild as an add-on summit during a full Bailey Range Traverse itinerary rather than a standalone objective — nearly everyone who climbs it is already out there for the traverse
watch_out: snow bridges over crevasses on the Fairchild/Carrie Glaciers that look solid but are undercut, especially after mid-August
losing the faint boot path on the exposed Catwalk section in fog or low visibility
underestimating the time commitment — this is realistically a 3-5 day objective, not a long day trip, even for strong parties

row.pro_needs: Glacier protection where snow/ice is present; minimal rock pro
row.best_season: Mid-July through mid-August is the truly optimal window — snow bridges over crevasses are still generally intact and steep sidehill sections in the Northern Baileys have softened enough to travel safely. Conditions remain feasible into early September, but glaciers run increasingly bare and icy (full crampon use, not microspikes) and snow bridges become less reliable; earlier in July, persistent steep snow on the Northern Baileys traverses can make travel more hazardous.
row.approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. At 0.8 mi pass Sol Duc Falls, and at 0.9 mi reach the Lovers Lane junction; branch left onto the Deer Lake Trail, which climbs steeply and relentlessly through switchbacks to Deer Lake (3.4 mi, ~3,527 ft) — the first reliable water and the last easy camping before things get serious. Beyond Deer Lake the trail continues up through Potholes Meadows (~5 mi) and gains the High Divide ridge crest around 6 mi/4,730 ft, with good views and intermittent tarns/snowmelt for water. At 7.4 mi pass the Seven Lakes Basin junction (4,900 ft) — a good last water/camp option — then continue along High Divide past or near Bogachiel Peak (5,474 ft). At roughly 10.2 mi, leave the maintained trail system at the Cat Basin junction; from here it is off-trail cross-country and boot-path travel only, dropping into Cat Basin below Cat Peak (5,940 ft) and then crossing the Catwalk, the narrow, exposed class 3 ridge linking Cat Peak to Mount Carrie (6,995 ft). Past it, many parties use the exposed, loose-talus sidehill traverse across Carrie's south face; an alternative preferred by some climbers is to stay higher on Carrie's north side, which avoids the worst sidehilling and leads up Carrie's ridge and upper flanks to its summit. The route to Fairchild starts from Mount Carrie's summit: head northeast down the Carrie Glacier (rope up and put on crampons here; ice axe mandatory most of the season), circle around to the north of Fairchild, and climb its Southwest Ridge to the 6,899 ft summit. This final section is only thinly described, so expect to find the line yourself. One-way distance to this point is roughly 12 miles with substantial cumulative gain from repeated up-and-down over Bogachiel Peak, Cat Peak, and the Carrie ridge system, consistent with the ~8,000 ft round-trip gain. Hazards: early-season creek crossings near Sol Duc Falls, steep loose-scree switchbacks on the Deer Lake Trail, serious exposure and loose rock on the Catwalk traverse, crevasses and snow bridges on the Carrie Glacier requiring roped glacier travel (especially early/mid-summer), no reliable water between Cat Basin and the glacier, and heavy route-finding demands in fog/whiteout since the entire Cat Basin-to-summit section is unmarked wilderness travel.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off/glacier-descent route with no rappelling. Descend by reversing the ascent line: from the summit, descend the Southwest Ridge, circle back around the north side of the peak and reclimb the Carrie Glacier roped up with crampons to Mount Carrie's summit, then descend Mount Carrie's north-side ridge. Sidehill back across Carrie's south face (or take the north-side alternative), then recross the Catwalk to Cat Basin, drop to rejoin the maintained High Divide Trail at the Cat Basin junction (~10.2 mi mark), and retrace the trail past the Seven Lakes Basin junction, Bogachiel Peak, Potholes Meadows, Deer Lake, and Lovers Lane back down to Sol Duc Falls and the Sol Duc River Trailhead. Some parties instead continue the descent onward as part of the broader Bailey Range Traverse — dropping south past Ruth Peak toward Stephen Lake/Queets Basin and exiting via the Elwha (Whiskey Bend) or Hoh River trailheads — but that is a different, longer one-way multi-day itinerary rather than the out-and-back standard route matching this route's distance and gain. Descent hazards mirror the approach: crevasse fall potential on the glacier (softening snow in the afternoon raises post-holing/slot risk, so an early turnaround is wise), loose talus on the Carrie sidehill, fatigue-driven route-finding errors in the featureless heather and scree of Cat Basin, and long, tired-legs reversal of the steep Deer Lake Trail switchbacks.
row.bail: Limited bail options - return along the approach

itinerary.cal: Best done mid-summer to early fall once the Long Creek ford is low and the glacier remnant is more open/less avalanche-prone; snow can linger on the approach ridges into July.

days.note: Start at the Whiskey Bend trailhead and follow the Elwha River Trail roughly 2 miles to Michaels Ranch, then turn onto the Long Ridge Trail, crossing the Elwha on a high suspension bridge before climbing steadily through forest onto the ridge. This maintained trail section gains several thousand feet and is the last easy walking of the trip.

access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters are mandatory for all overnight off-trail camping in the Bailey Range.
access.permit: NPS wilderness camping permit required for any overnight stay in the Bailey Range; reserve on Recreation.gov (summer-season permits typically release around mid-April) or through the Wilderness Information Center, (360) 565-3100.
access.closures: Sol Duc Road closes seasonally in winter/early spring — check the NPS road-conditions line (360-565-3131) or nps.gov/olym road-conditions page before driving in. The Bailey Range route itself is generally only safely passable from roughly July through September.

climate.fall: Conditions deteriorate quickly after mid-September with increasing rain, wind, and early snow.
climate.spring: Heavy snowpack lingers into early summer; the Catwalk and glacier crossing are typically not viable until snow consolidates.
climate.summer: July-September is the reliable weather and access window, though rain and wind can still arrive with little warning.
climate.winter: Not a winter objective — access roads close seasonally and the range holds a deep, unstable snowpack.
climate.typical: The Bailey Range interior sees more precipitation and cloud cover than the rain-shadow towns north of the park but less than the drenched western river valleys; persistent snowfields commonly linger into July even in average years.

bySeason.summer: Prime climbing window mid-July through early September; best conditions (intact snow bridges, softer sidehill snow) are mid-July to mid-August.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC issues an 'Olympics' avalanche/mountain-weather zone forecast, but NWAC only operates in winter (roughly mid-November through mid-April) — for summer climbing conditions, use NWS point forecasts for the area plus recent trip reports.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage anywhere in the Bailey Range interior; carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT). Serious trauma cases are typically evacuated by helicopter (Olympic NP SAR / Airlift Northwest) to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle.
emergency.rangerStation: Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center (Port Angeles), (360) 565-3100
emergency.nearestHospital: Olympic Medical Center (Olympic Memorial Hospital), 939 Caroline St, Port Angeles — roughly 2+ hours' drive from the Sol Duc Trailhead, considerably farther from interior camps

crowds.peakTraffic: Rare even in peak summer (late July-August); trip reports on the Bailey Range consistently describe seeing few or no other parties once past the Sol Duc/Cat Walk approach, though the approach trails themselves (Sol Duc past Heart Lake, Sol Duc Falls) see real hiker/tourist traffic
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low - likely well under 20 parties per season summit Fairchild itself; it's usually a side-objective off the Bailey Range Traverse rather than a standalone destination

August.reason: The best window - snow has cleared from most of the route and the long approach is most reliable

weather.typical: Interior Olympics climate: heavy winter snowpack with long approaches; best window is mid-July through early September once snow clears
weather.probability: Pacific frontal systems can bring sudden weather changes even in summer, and early storms are a fall risk; with the remoteness, there is very limited escape if weather turns

approach_variants.notes: Sol Duc to Deer Lake, up through Potholes Meadows onto the High Divide crest and past Bogachiel Peak, leaving maintained trail at the Cat Basin junction around ten miles. From there it is boot path and cross-country below Cat Peak and around Mount Carrie. Almost every ascent happens mid-traverse rather than as a standalone climb.
hazards: Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Fairchild Glacier, worse late season
Bare, hard glacier ice by late summer needing full crampon technique
Severe exposure and loose talus on the sidehill traverse across Carrie
No dependable water between Cat Basin and the glacier
Route-finding across largely featureless post-glacial ground in whiteout
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base here is a glacier entry rather than a rock step, and the marker is a snow feature. From Cat Basin, climb or sidehill around Mount Carrie — the higher line on Carrie's north side avoids the worst of the traverse and sets up a cleaner entry than the exposed sidehill does. Aim to reach the upper Fairchild Glacier at roughly 6,700 ft on the northeast side of the Carrie–Fairchild ridge. You are in the right place when a wind-formed snow ridge runs away down the glacier ahead of you: a firm raised spine, much like a hogsback, and it exists precisely because following it keeps you clear of the crevassed ground on either side. Rope up and put crampons on before stepping onto it, not once you are committed. Lower, flatter snow aprons on the same flank look like easier entries and lead into broken ice, so do not take the first snow you meet. Near the summit ridge the spine steepens to something like 35 to 40 degrees beside an icy patch — that is the correct exit rather than a sign you are off line. Bare rock and moraine underfoot means you are still below the glacier.

bivy.name: Eleven Bull Basin and the Cream Lake cross-country camps
bivy.notes: These are the working camps for Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild. Eleven Bull Basin sits beneath Carrie and Ruth, a meadow with running streams, and it is the natural second night for a party that climbed Carrie from Boston Charlie's. Fairchild is the next peak along the crest, less than a mile north of Ruth, and both are class 3 from this side. Beyond, the route continues toward Ferry Basin and eventually Glacier Pass, which is the only way Mount Mathias is reached from this end — several more days of committing off-trail travel, some of it on glacier. Water dictates the itinerary here far more than distance does, so plan camps around the basins rather than around mileage.
bivy.water: Good in Eleven Bull Basin, where streams run out of the hillside most of the season; sparse between there and Cream Lake, and Cream Lake itself is swampy and buggy enough that many parties take the higher bypass toward Stephen Lake instead
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, arranged by phone with the park's wilderness information office — these are not campsites you can pick off the online map. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned, and the leave-no-trace expectation is stricter here than at any designated camp because nothing is hardened.
bivy.capacity: Dispersed cross-country camping in meadow basins; no designated sites, no toilets, and no capacity beyond what the ground will take without damage

bivy.name: Cat Basin
bivy.notes: Cat Basin lies just below the junction at roughly 5,042 ft where the High Divide trail meets the way into the Bailey Range, so it is the last sheltered ground on the approach before the route turns cross-country beneath Cat Peak. Parties heading for Mount Carrie use it to shorten the following morning and to get below the wind, since the divide itself is fully exposed. It is genuinely primitive — expect to be finding your own flat spot on durable ground, and expect the sites to be scattered rather than obvious. In heavy snow years the basin fills late and the traverse out to the Catwalk holds steep snow well into July.
bivy.water: Streams in the basin early in the season, unreliable by late summer; carry from Heart Lake if the year has been dry
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required. This one is worth phoning the park's wilderness information office about rather than assuming — the primitive and cross-country parts of this area are not all bookable through the standard online map, and staff issue those permits directly. Bear canisters mandatory, campfires banned outright at this height.
bivy.capacity: A primitive designated area rather than a developed camp; a handful of tent spots, no toilet you should count on

bivy.name: Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort campground
bivy.notes: The drive-in staging base for every objective in this zone except Mount Angeles, a couple of miles short of the end of the Sol Duc Hot Springs Road where the trailhead for the High Divide and Appleton Pass sits. Climbers use it the night before, because the walk to Heart Lake or Appleton Pass is long enough that leaving Port Angeles in the morning wastes the day. It opens with the season, roughly late March into late October, and it fills solidly on summer weekends. It is a staging base and nothing more — from here you still have the entire approach ahead of you, and every camp above it is permit-controlled.
bivy.water: Potable water and flush toilets in the comfort stations through the operating season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — this is a frontcountry campground with a nightly fee, taken on the federal recreation booking site or through the resort. Park entrance fee applies. Fires are allowed in the provided rings here, unlike anywhere you are going above it.
bivy.capacity: Around 82 tent sites plus a smaller RV loop; most tent sites are reservable and a handful are held back first-come

bivy.name: Deer Lake
bivy.notes: Three and a half miles up from the Sol Duc trailhead by way of Sol Duc Falls, this is the first camp on the loop and the one parties take when they get away late and cannot face the climb to Heart Lake in the dark. For a Bailey Range objective it is a poor base on its own — you are still well below the High Divide and four or more miles short of where the cross-country travel starts — so treat it as a way of splitting the walk in rather than as a summit camp. Its low elevation and lake make it the most forgiving camp in the zone in bad weather, and it holds snow later into the spring than its height suggests.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake itself, plus Canyon Creek on the way up; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and this is a QUOTA camp reserved for a specific night on the federal booking site. Approved bear canisters are mandatory throughout the Sol Duc, High Divide and Seven Lakes Basin area. Campfires are banned — nothing above 3,500 ft in this park may have one, and this camp sits right at that line.
bivy.capacity: A modest cluster of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; parties of seven or more must use a designated group site

bivy.name: Heart Lake
bivy.notes: The most useful camp in the whole zone for a climber. It sits just under eight miles in, a short climb below the High Divide, and it is the last camp on maintained trail with easy water before the route to Mount Carrie, Ruth Peak and Mount Fairchild leaves the trail for good. From here you gain the divide, follow it past Cat Peak, cross the exposed class 3 ridge known as the Catwalk, and the climbing starts. Parties who miss the permit sometimes take a Seven Lakes Basin camp such as Lunch Lake instead, but that puts you off the direct line and adds side-hilling in the morning. Fill every bottle here — the stretch from the divide out to the first Bailey Range camps carries no running water.
bivy.water: Reliable — the lake and the creek feeding it, all season; this is the last dependable running water for a long way
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, QUOTA camp booked for a specific night on the federal booking site. Reservations for the summer season open in the spring and the High Divide camps are among the fastest to go in the park, often within minutes. Bear canisters mandatory, no campfires.
bivy.capacity: A small number of designated sites under a nightly cap, with a vault toilet; group parties must use the designated group site

bivy.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
bivy.notes: This is the first camp on the far side of the Catwalk and the recognised start of the Bailey Range proper. It matters because it puts you directly at the foot of Mount Carrie's southwest ridge, where the route gains around 2,000 ft in under a mile on a semi-cairned bootpack, so a party camped here can be on the summit early and off the loose ground before the afternoon. Getting to it means crossing the exposed class 3 ridge between Cat Peak and Carrie with a full pack, which is the crux of the approach for most people and not somewhere to be in wet weather. The water is the honest drawback and the reason some parties push straight through to the basins beyond.
bivy.water: Poor and the standing complaint about the place — a shallow sinkhole pond that is often silty and stagnant, and nothing else nearby. Filter and treat, and consider carrying from Heart Lake or Cat Basin
bivy.permit: Covered by an Olympic wilderness cross-country permit, which for the Bailey Range is arranged directly with the park's wilderness information office rather than booked as a named campsite online. Bear canisters mandatory. No fires. Camp on durable surfaces — snow, rock or gravel — and pack out everything.
bivy.capacity: Informal cross-country bivy sites for a couple of small parties; no facilities of any kind

row.overview: Mount Dana (6,213 ft, ~1,529 ft prominence) is an isolated, trailless summit in the Bailey Range, part of Olympic National Park's rugged interior above the headwaters of the Elwha River. It was named by the 1889-90 Seattle Press Expedition — the party that first explored the Olympic interior and named most of the Bailey Range — for Charles A. Dana, an editor of the New York Sun. The first recorded ascent was in 1928 by a USGS survey party. The peak is built of Eocene-age basalt typical of the Olympic core rocks, and its nearest higher neighbor is Mount Norton (6,397 ft), about 3.9 miles away. There is no maintained trail anywhere near the summit; climbers reach it only as a side excursion from a multi-day Bailey Range or Elwha-interior traverse, making it one of the more committing sub-6,500-ft summits in the park.
row.beta: Mount Dana's only recorded route is a straightforward scramble; it is classified simply as 'scrambling' with no formal class rating published, and it lacks the pitch-by-pitch detail that exists for the main Bailey Range Traverse peaks. Most parties reach the Bailey Range crest via the Elwha River Trail and travel off-trail; an alternate approach along the ridge from Mount Barnes to Dana reportedly involves exposed downclimbing, but this has not been formally written up. Treat this as a route-finding, self-sufficient objective rather than a beta-rich one.
row.turnaround: Because this is a remote, off-trail objective with no maintained trail nearby and a multi-day approach, set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight and weather margin to retreat all the way back to the Bailey Range crest and down to the Elwha corridor, not just off the summit itself.
row.permit: Olympic National Park: no permit for day climbs; all overnight wilderness stays require a wilderness camping permit via Recreation.gov.
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage should be expected in the Elwha/Bailey Range interior; general park guidance notes coverage is scarce to nonexistent in Olympic National Park's remote backcountry even at higher points like Hurricane Ridge, with Verizon reported as the least-bad option elsewhere in the park. Carry a satellite communicator for this objective.

pro_tips: Plan as a multi-day trip with a park wilderness permit
Strong navigation skills needed on the off-trail sections
Call the Wilderness Information Center (360-565-3100) for current Elwha Snow Finger conditions before relying on it as your route through Dodwell-Rixon Pass.
row.approach: Getting to the trailhead is part of the approach: November 2017 flood damage closed Olympic Hot Springs Road to vehicles at the Madison Falls parking area, and that closure, still listed with no reopening date on Olympic National Park's alerts page updated August 27, 2026, adds roughly 7 miles each way of road walking or biking just to reach the Whiskey Bend trailhead (the road remains open to foot/bike traffic beyond Madison Falls). From Whiskey Bend, the actual hike-in follows the Elwha River Trail, a well-graded historic path along the river's east bank that passes the old Geyser Valley homestead sites (Michael's Cabin, Humes Ranch) in the first mile or two. The trail is mellow by Olympic standards, staying under roughly 2,000 ft of gain through its first 15+ miles, and passes Lillian River junction (~4 mi), Mary's Falls Camp (8.8 mi), Canyon Camp, Elkhorn Guard Station, and Stony Point as it winds upstream through old-growth forest with the Elwha River itself as a constant, reliable water source. Camp Wilder and Hayes River Guard Station mark roughly the trail's halfway point. Continue south to Elwha Basin and Chicago Camp (roughly 24-26 trail miles from Whiskey Bend), where the Elwha River must be forded — NPS explicitly flags this crossing as one to check conditions on beforehand, since it can be genuinely hazardous in early-season high water or after rain. At and beyond Chicago Camp the maintained trail effectively dissolves into the Elwha Basin, and travel becomes cross-country: a boot-beaten climbers' path continues up the valley headwaters toward the obvious white tongue of the Elwha Snow Finger, a permanent, avalanche-fed snowfield filling the bedrock gully that leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass (4,763'). The Snow Finger is the standard way through this section — carry an ice axe and know self-arrest. Recent parties note the snowpack has been thinning in late summer, exposing an opening moat, running water under the snow, and rockfall funneling off the surrounding walls, so climb it early in the day and reassess if it looks broken up; NPS notes snow can linger above Chicago Camp into July. From the top of the Snow Finger at Dodwell-Rixon Pass, Mount Dana sits several miles east-northeast (its coordinates place it roughly 5 miles from the pass, closer to the Mount Norton/Elwha-headwaters side of the range than to the main Carrie-Ferry-Pulitzer crest). There is no path here; parties pick a line across talus, heather benches, and lingering snow patches toward Dana's western slopes for the final class 2 scramble to the 6,214' summit. Water becomes scarce above the pass, so carry enough for a high camp. Given the roughly 70-mile round-trip distance, this is realistically a multi-day trip (3+ days) with a high camp near Dodwell-Rixon Pass or in the upper Elwha basin, not a car-to-car push, and solid off-trail navigation skill is essential once you're past Chicago Camp.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off/scramble-down — no rappelling is documented (or generally needed) on Mount Dana or on the standard Dodwell-Rixon Pass access route. From the summit, reverse the ascent line: cross-country back west-southwest over the talus and heather benches to Dodwell-Rixon Pass, then down-climb the Elwha Snow Finger as the return route to Elwha Basin/Chicago Camp. Descending the Snow Finger is generally more hazard-prone than climbing it — a glissade is tempting on a mellow day but should be avoided if the moat at the base is open, if the surface has softened into slush, or if there's a risk of sliding into exposed rock (trip reports from this same drainage describe a nearby 'crevasse-like gap' where a stream undercuts the snow), so plan to face in and down-climb with an axe ready for self-arrest anywhere it steepens, particularly late season when the finger has thinned and pulled away from the surrounding rock walls. Below the snow, pick up the boot path back to Chicago Camp, re-ford the Elwha River, and rejoin the maintained Elwha River Trail for the long, gentle walk back down-valley (~24-26 miles) to Whiskey Bend — plus the current ~7-mile road walk/bike back to Madison Falls while the Olympic Hot Springs Road washout remains unrepaired. No technical anchors, fixed or natural, come into play anywhere on this route; the real crux of the descent is correctly reading the Snow Finger's snow condition and the scree/talus around the pass, not rope work.
row.bail: Descend to the nearest interior trail and follow it out.

climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: the Olympics wring heavy precipitation out of Pacific storm fronts forced upward by the range. Winters bring heavy, wet snow with high avalanche danger; summers are comparatively clear and are the only realistic climbing window.

row.rope_note: Little is published about this peak specifically, so treat it as a route-finding, self-sufficient objective rather than a beta-rich one and carry navigation before you carry hardware: map, compass and a GPS track for extensive off-trail travel. Nothing here is rappelled and no rack is needed. An ice axe early season, and crampons if snow or ice is sitting on the Elwha Snow Finger or the approach gullies, are what the terrain actually asks for, along with a helmet and footwear you can ford a river in. Descending the Snow Finger is more hazard-prone than climbing it, so check its condition before you commit to it as your way back.

bivy.name: Elwha Basin, Queets Basin and the upper cross-country bivy zones
bivy.notes: This is the working base for the Elwha Basin peaks and the only sensible way to reach the Bailey Range from the south. From Chicago Camp the route into Elwha Basin is a notorious bushwhack in low snow years, then the Elwha Snowfinger leads to Dodwell-Rixon Pass at 4,763 ft and over into Queets Basin. From a basin camp, MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT NOYES and MOUNT QUEETS are all short days, MOUNT MEANY is usually taken from Seattle Basin or over the Noyes-Meany col, and a further push west from Queets Basin puts MOUNT FERRY and MOUNT PULITZER within reach. Season is everything: the snowfinger in good condition is fast and pleasant, and the same ground in September is loose talus and alder. There is no shelter, no toilet and no established site, so pick ground that will not be flooded and leave nothing. If your party is not comfortable making its own camp on unimproved terrain, this zone is not the right objective.
bivy.water: Meltwater and snow. Abundant early, and increasingly a question by late summer once the snowfinger and the basin streams shrink — carry capacity rather than assuming the next creek is running.
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required and CROSS-COUNTRY ZONES CANNOT BE BOOKED ONLINE — you must telephone the wilderness information centre, and the rangers will ask about your experience before issuing. Name every zone you intend to sleep in; one permit follows you between zones on a multi-day route. Bear canister mandatory. No campfires above 3,500 ft, so this is a stove-only zone. Human waste should be buried well away from meltwater or packed out on snow and rock.
bivy.capacity: No designated sites — these are cross-country zones and parties camp on whatever flat gravel, heather bench or moraine they reach; groups are small by necessity

bivy.name: Chicago Camp — the last established camp in the upper Elwha
bivy.notes: Chicago Camp is where the trail effectively ends and the cross-country begins, roughly twenty-five miles from Whiskey Bend at the confluence of the Elwha and Delabarre Creek. It is the standard last-trail-camp for MOUNT BARNES, MOUNT MEANY, MOUNT NOYES, MOUNT QUEETS and MOUNT WILDER, all of which are reached by pushing on into the Elwha Basin above. The ford at the camp can be genuinely hazardous in high water and is the crux of the walk in for many parties. A short way beyond, the upper Elwha has a cave-like recess under an overhanging wall that has served as emergency shelter for generations, but it is a bolthole and not a camp. Camping here rather than in the basin costs you three miles and a couple of thousand feet on summit day; the trade is a sheltered site with running water and a defined trail underfoot, which matters more than it sounds after four days of walking.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha and Delabarre Creek meet here
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. It is more than fifteen miles from any road, and the booking system does not always surface camps that far in, so ring the wilderness information centre rather than assuming it is unavailable. Bear canister mandatory. No fires above 3,500 ft, which applies once you climb out of here.
bivy.capacity: Small, and it has been battered by fallen timber — expect only a couple of usable sites near the river

bivy.name: Lillian River and Mary's Falls — the first night out of Whiskey Bend
bivy.notes: The whole Elwha approach now begins with a road walk, and it is the single biggest change to planning in this valley. Vehicles stop at the Madison Falls parking area; the Olympic Hot Springs Road and then the Whiskey Bend Road are closed by a washout that has stood for years with no repair date, which puts the old Whiskey Bend trailhead about six to seven miles away on foot. The park's own figure is seven. Bicycles are allowed on the closed road and cut that leg to well under an hour each way, and most parties heading deep now ride it and stash a bike. Lillian River is around four and a half miles past Whiskey Bend and Mary's Falls a little further, so either one turns a brutal first day into a civilised one when you are carrying enough food for a week in the interior. Going higher on day one is possible but you gain nothing except a shorter second day; the elevation profile of the Elwha barely rises for the first fifteen miles.
bivy.water: Reliable at both — the Lillian River at one, the Elwha at the other; treat everything
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance on the federal recreation site. These lower Elwha camps are not inside a quota area, so they are usually obtainable late, but no sites anywhere in this park are held back as same-day walk-ups. Bear canister mandatory. Fires are allowed at this elevation but the Elwha and every tributary are closed to fishing.
bivy.capacity: Lillian River has roughly six roomy riverside sites; Mary's Falls is smaller and set in maple and grass with the river some way off

bivy.name: Hayes River and Elkhorn — the mid-valley camps, and the base for Mount Norton
bivy.notes: Elkhorn sits about eleven miles up the Elwha from Whiskey Bend and Hayes River about sixteen, both on level ground and both far more pleasant than Canyon Camp between them, which has been badly hit by treefall and is worth walking past. Hayes River is the camp for MOUNT NORTON: the peak's east side rises roughly 3,200 ft straight out of the Hayes River drainage in under a mile, and the ascent is a steep off-trail slog rather than a climb. It is also the last comfortable place to sleep before the valley narrows, so parties bound for Chicago Camp and the Elwha Basin peaks routinely take it as night two. Going further the same day is a real option in long daylight but the trail past Camp Wilder deteriorates and the camps beyond are rougher. Bugs are heavy in the meadows from late June into July.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Elwha at Elkhorn, the Hayes River at Hayes; both run all season
bivy.permit: Olympic wilderness permit required, booked in advance. Not a quota area, so these are among the easier permits in the park to obtain at short notice. Bear canister mandatory.
bivy.capacity: Both are spacious grassy flats with several sites each, alongside old guard stations that are usually empty; they are the least contested camps in the valley

A documented 5-day loop matches the itinerary exactly (Robinson Creek TH -> Middle Fork flats -> Rolo/Shellrock -> North Monument Creek pond -> Butte Pass/Pass Butte/Lost -> Lake of the Woods -> Pistol Pass -> Eureka Falls -> Monument TH), and the Forest Service confirms the Monument Creek trail beyond Eureka Creek is unmaintained. All three lines are real ways to reach the peak, so choosing one and rewriting the approach, descent, waypoints and itinerary to it is a restructuring decision, not a minimal patch. row.overview: Lost Peak (8,464 ft, 1,624 ft prominence) sits in the Okanogan Range of the North Cascades, about 16 miles north of Mazama and 7 miles northwest of Big Craggy Peak, deep in the interior of the Pasayten Wilderness. It ranks among Washington's 100 highest peaks. There is no trail to the summit — it lies several cross-country miles beyond the nearest maintained trail, so most parties combine it with nearby Pass Butte and/or the Lago group (Mt. Lago, Mt. Carru, Osceola Peak, Blackcap Peak) on a multi-day loop rather than climbing it in isolation. Lage Wernstedt, the USFS topographer credited with numerous early Pasayten first ascents (nearby Dot Mountain is named for his wife, Dottie), is credited with the first ascent in 1925.
row.beta: Lost Peak has no technical climbing routes. The standard (and essentially only documented) line ascends loose scree/talus on the southwest slope at Class 3. Parties approaching from the north often traverse in from Pass Butte along the connecting ridge/slopes to avoid the worst of the scree found on the south and southwest aspects, then descend via the southwest slope/ridge. Because the approach is 20+ miles round trip through unmaintained trail on parts of the route, most parties treat this as a 3-day wilderness backpack rather than a day climb.
row.turnaround: Set a hard summit-day turnaround (e.g., early afternoon): the ridge above Butte Pass has no shelter from thunderstorms, and finding the way back to camp through cross-country terrain is much harder in fog, dark, or storm.
row.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead; no quota or fee. Northwest Forest Pass at some trailheads.
row.comms: No reliable cell coverage in this part of the Pasayten Wilderness backcountry; a satellite messenger (inReach/SPOT) is recommended for the multi-day approach.
row.descent: Descend by reversing the ascent line off the summit via the southwest/northwest ridge, down loose talus and scree back to Butte Pass or the North Monument Creek basin, then retrace the multi-day approach trail out. No rappels are required on the standard scramble route; the main descent hazard is controlling scree underfoot and avoiding rockfall onto party members below.
obj_haz: early/late-season snow and possible cornices on north-facing gullies
swift snowmelt fords of North Monument Creek and Eureka Creek
afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline
remote self-rescue distance — multi-day from any trailhead or road

waypoints.name: Monument Creek Trailhead (Lost River Road / Harts Pass Road)
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead on Lost River Road (FR 5400 spur); no parking pass needed; fill out the free self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk, last reliable water/toilet before miles of Pasayten trail.

waypoints.name: Robinson Pass
waypoints.note: Gains the Middle Fork Pasayten divide via a steep final 1.2-mile forested pitch; trail forks here toward the Pasayten River valley.
waypoints.directions: Trail #478 follows Robinson Creek through big timber for about six miles, never far from the sound of the water, then fords the creek. Above the ford the grade stays gradual through forest, crossing several avalanche runouts, and breaks into meadowland near 4,700 ft. Pass the Slate Pass Trail junction and finish with a half mile of open meadow climbing to the pass.

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Pasayten River flats
waypoints.note: Common first-night camp beside the river a few miles below Robinson Pass; reliable water but mosquito-heavy in early season.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass and descend about three miles into the broad U-shaped Middle Fork valley, losing roughly 1,800 ft to river level. Camps sit along the water here.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.note: Green alpine lake ringed by larches with a popular established camp; last dependable water before the Rolo/Shellrock high country.
waypoints.directions: Continue down-river before the trail turns and climbs back into the high country, gaining around 2,100 ft to the lake basin. Fred's Lake sits a short way off the main trail rather than on it, so watch for the spur or you will walk straight past it.

waypoints.name: Rolo Pass
waypoints.note: Ridge-crest pass just above Fred's Lake; route continues cross-country toward the head of Eureka Creek and Shellrock Basin.
waypoints.directions: From the lake keep climbing to the ridge-crest pass a few hundred feet above, through open larch and talus. The maintained tread thins out above the lake, and this is where the route stops being a trail hike.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Pass / Shellrock Basin
waypoints.note: Trail here has been unmaintained for decades and the basin fogs in frequently; easy to lose the faint tread in whiteout, navigate by map/compass.
waypoints.directions: From Rolo Pass drop to the headwaters of Eureka Creek and traverse across into Shellrock Basin, then climb to the pass at 7,500 ft. The tread through here has been unmaintained for decades and is faint to nonexistent, and the basin fogs in readily — carry map and compass and be ready to navigate without seeing any of the surrounding peaks.

waypoints.name: Lost Peak
waypoints.note: Class 3 talus/meadow scramble up the southwest or northwest ridge from a Shellrock Pass area camp; descend the same ridge line reversed.
waypoints.directions: From a camp near the pass, gain either the southwest or the northwest ridge and follow it over talus and alpine meadow to the top. Class 3 with no sustained technical ground, but the crest is high, exposed to wind, and can hold snow well past midsummer.

what_to_bring: free self-issue wilderness permit (fill out at the trailhead register)
topo map + compass or GPS/inReach — much of the route is cross-country with no trail
layers for wind-exposed, cold ridges even in July/August
pro_tips: Combine with Pass Butte and/or the Lago group (Osceola, Carru, Lago, Blackcap) via Shellrock Pass — the approach is long enough that most parties make a multi-peak trip of it
Camp near Butte Pass or North Monument Creek to shorten summit day and minimize time on the loose southwest-slope scree
Verify current Harts Pass Road status before committing to a trip — access to the standard trailheads has been unreliable due to storm damage
watch_out: numerous false summits/points along the ridge before the true summit — a commonly reported frustration on the approach
cross-country ledge and ridge sections above Butte Pass/Shellrock Pass have no cairns or trail
loose talus and scree on the south/southwest slopes — the Butte Pass line avoids the worst of it
row.pro_needs: Easy class 2 scramble; no technical gear normally required.
row.best_season: Mid-July through September. Snow lingers on north-facing terrain and passes into early-mid July in an average year; one late-September (9/22-9/26) party found the high ridges around Lost Peak snowy, cold, and wind-blasted, with early-season alpine conditions, so shoulder-season parties should be ready for winter-like weather above treeline.
row.approach: Lost Peak sits deep in the Pasayten Wilderness and the standard approach is a serious backcountry undertaking, not a day hike from a roadside trailhead. From the Monument Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft, off Lost River Road) follow Monument Creek Trail #484, which is well-maintained through old-growth forest for the first ~4 miles along Monument Creek and the Lost River — water is plentiful here and this stretch is even rideable by mountain bike, which some parties use to bank easy miles before caching bikes at the wilderness boundary. At roughly mile 4 the maintained tread ends at a washed-out bridge over Eureka Creek; beyond this point the trail has not been maintained in 25-30 years and becomes a faint, brushy, deadfall-choked route requiring solid navigation and a ford of Eureka Creek. Continue up the Monument Creek drainage (on-and-off tread, increasingly cross-country) into the North Monument Creek basin, where parties commonly camp at a small pond/tarn below Butte Pass — this is roughly 16+ miles in and the practical base camp for the peak (an alternate approach comes in from Robinson Creek/Shellrock Pass to the south, about 21.5 miles, used on longer Pasayten-Eleven traverses). From camp, climb to Butte Pass, then follow the ridge directly up to Pass Butte (~8,140 ft). From Pass Butte, continue along the connecting ridge over the col near Point 8107 and southeast across several false summits — Class 2 talus and rock scrambling, reported as 'quite fun' underfoot with mostly firm dirt/talus rather than loose scree — to Lost Peak's summit. Given the recorded ~77 km round-trip distance, this route is essentially always done as a multi-day backpack with the peak tagged as a day-scramble from high camp, not car-to-car. Hazards: the unmarked, unmaintained trail beyond Eureka Creek with brush and deadfall; the Eureka Creek ford; remote terrain with no cell coverage; a long, navigation-heavy ridge walk with numerous false summits that is easy to get wrong in poor visibility; and lingering snow or sudden weather on the high, exposed ridge even in summer.
row.descent_text: This is a walk-off/downclimb scramble descent with no rappelling — reverse the Class 2 ridge scramble back over the false summits to the col near Point 8107, back along the connecting ridge to Pass Butte, and down to Butte Pass and camp. At least one documented party descended via a west-ridge variant instead of a strict reversal while staying in radio contact with other group members, so there is some flexibility in the exact line off the summit ridge, but no technical gear or fixed anchors are involved either way. The main descent hazards are the same navigation difficulty as the ascent — multiple false summits and a broad ridge crest that can be disorienting in whiteout, wind, or after dark (one party topped out near 8:45 PM and descended by headlamp) — plus the standard alpine risks of afternoon thunderstorms and residual snow patches on the exposed ridge. From camp, the return to the trailhead simply reverses the ~16+ mile approach down Monument Creek, re-fording Eureka Creek and picking the maintained tread back up for the final 4 miles to the trailhead.
row.bail: The standard route has no technical downclimbing or rappels, so bailing off the peak itself is straightforward in good weather. The real commitment is the multi-day cross-country approach — retreating from deep in the North Monument Creek/Shellrock Pass basin in bad weather is slow, so build in extra food/fuel days rather than pushing a closing weather window.

pitch_detail.notes: Multi-day trail approach (roughly 9-11+ miles one-way over Robinson Pass or to Pistol Pass, depending on trailhead) including unmaintained trail sections and an Eureka Creek ford, to a high camp near Butte Pass or Shellrock Pass.
Loose scree/talus scramble up the southwest slope to the 8,464-ft summit; often linked with Pass Butte via a connecting ridge traverse from the north.

itinerary.cal: Pasayten Wilderness trailheads and high passes typically aren't fully clear of snow until mid-to-late July; this is a self-issue wilderness permit area with no advance reservation needed.

itinerary.totalNote: A full 5-day, roughly 48-mile loop backpack (~14,000 ft cumulative gain) through the Pasayten Wilderness, with one dedicated summit day linking Pass Butte and Lost Peak from a high camp near Shellrock/Butte Pass; Lost Peak's remoteness rules out a single-day car-to-car approach.

access.fees: No wilderness entry fee; no parking pass is needed at the Monument Creek or Slate Pass trailheads, but parking at the Robinson Creek trailhead requires a Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass.
access.rules: Group size capped at 12 people / 18 head of stock.
access.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the trailhead register (no quota, no reservation, no cost).
access.closures: Harts Pass Road (Lost River Rd / FR 9140 -> FR 5400) was closed to vehicles from the Monument Creek Trailhead through Harts Pass after storm/flood damage in December 2025, cutting off the Robinson Creek, Slate Pass, and Slate Peak trailheads used for the standard approaches; it was listed open again by the Forest Service as of July 2, 2026. Separately, the Ptarmigan Fire closure (Forest Service order 06-17-04-26-39, in effect September 9 through October 31, 2026) closes Monument Creek Trail #484 north of the Lake of the Woods turnoff, Eureka Creek Trail #474, Robinson Creek Trail #478 north of Eureka Creek, and Buckskin Ridge Trail #498; Methow Valley Ranger District, (509) 996-4000. Verify current status with the Methow Valley Ranger District before planning a trip.

road.name: Harts Pass Road (Lost River Rd -> FR 9140 -> FR 5400)
road.status: Open; closed to vehicles from the Monument Creek Trailhead through Harts Pass after December 2025 storm/flood damage, and listed open again by the Forest Service as of July 2, 2026 (closed to trailers in summer).
road.driveNote: From Winthrop, WA drive about 15 miles west on Highway 20, turn onto Lost River Road (County Road 9140), continue on pavement then gravel FR 5400 to reach the Robinson Creek or Monument Creek trailheads. The road has a recent history of multi-month storm-damage closures beyond Monument Creek Trailhead — check current Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest alerts before driving in.
road.seasonalGate: In a normal (non-storm-damage) year the road and Harts Pass typically open to vehicles by early-mid summer (around the Fourth of July); high-elevation portions can hold snow into June.

climate.fall: Cool and often clear, with larch color in nearby basins by late September, but increasing chance of early-season snow.
climate.spring: Snowbound through at least June at these elevations; access road/trails typically not clear until late June.
climate.summer: Warm to hot days with cool nights; afternoon thunderstorms are common in the high country.
climate.winter: Heavy snow and cold; the peak and access roads are effectively inaccessible.
climate.typical: Dry, sunnier east-slope-Cascades climate compared to the west side, but still exposed and cold at elevation — expect cold nights and possible summer thunderstorms even in August. Snow can linger on north aspects and passes into early-mid July.

bySeason.fall: Larches turn gold in Eureka Creek/Shellrock Basin in late September, but a documented late-Sept trip found the high ridges already "snowy, cold, and wind-blasted" — treat late season as shoulder winter conditions.
bySeason.spring: Passes and approach trails are typically snow-covered and not practical for this route.
bySeason.summer: Late July through September is the reliable snow-free window for the high passes (Rolo, Shellrock, Butte); a normal winter clears most routes by early-mid July.
bySeason.winter: Not a winter objective — Harts Pass Road and interior trails are snowbound and the wilderness is essentially inaccessible.

emergency.notes: No cell coverage in the Pasayten interior; this is genuine multi-day self-rescue country far from any road. Carry a satellite communicator (inReach/SPOT) and leave a detailed trip plan. Aero Methow Rescue Service (Winthrop-based) provides EMS/ambulance response for the Methow Valley, typically dispatched via Okanogan County 911.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA 98862 — (509) 996-4000 (permits, current trail/road conditions)
emergency.nearestHospital: Three Rivers Hospital, Brewster (509-689-2517) or Mid-Valley Hospital, Omak (509-826-1760) — both roughly an hour's drive from the Methow Valley
emergency.sheriffDispatch: 911 for emergencies; Okanogan County Sheriff non-emergency/dispatch (509) 422-7232 opt. 4

crowds.peakTraffic: Late July-August, and almost always bundled into longer peakbagging loops rather than climbed alone
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Unknown precise count, likely well under 20 parties/season - trip reports found are sparse and nearly all describe Lost Peak as one summit tagged during multi-day, multi-peak Pasayten loops (e.g. with Pass Butte, Blackcap, Ptarmigan, Osceola) rather than a standalone objective

fitnessSpec.hiking: Strong multi-day backpacking fitness - proven approaches run 11+ miles one-way to Pistol Pass, and loop trip reports log 40+ miles with 13,000+ ft gain over several days
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Multi-day wilderness pack (food/shelter/navigation for a several-day trip); no technical climbing gear required beyond standard scrambling kit

partner_requirements.approachTime: Long, multi-day approach - shortest proven line follows Lost River-Monument Creek-Ptarmigan Creek Trail toward Pistol Peaks, reaching 7,100-ft Pistol Pass at roughly 11 miles before off-trail travel to the summit; most parties do it as part of a several-day Pasayten loop
requiredSkills: Off-trail Class 2 (locally Class 3/4 to bypass a summit snowfield) route-finding through talus and past false summits
Self-sufficient wilderness navigation - long, remote approach with no cell coverage or quick bail-out
Basic snow travel/kick-stepping for the summit snowfield when present
Self-rescue mindset given the extreme remoteness
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced wilderness backpacker/scrambler comfortable with multi-day off-trail travel far from help; described in trip reports as an 'unremarkable' Washington Top-100/Bulger peak usually combined with several other Pasayten summits in one trip, so partners should be prepared for a big multi-day itinerary, not a single-day tag

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Mid-July through September - narrowing further, snow lingers on approach terrain into early July and stable weather is most reliable August through mid-September

July.reason: Window opens mid-July; early July can still have lingering snow and high water on the long approach

June.reason: Approach trails and off-trail slopes still snow-covered; high creek crossings likely

August.reason: Prime dry window for this drier continental NE Cascades climate; best combination of stable weather and melted-out terrain

October.reason: Early-season storms become likely, and this is far outside the best-season window

September.reason: Stable but shorter days; early storms are possible later in the month

weather.typical: Drier continental NE Cascades climate - drier east-side conditions in summer, stable but short days in fall
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer; exposed ridge/summit terrain on this deep-wilderness route raises the stakes of getting caught out

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate - Class 2 talus and ridge travel with false summits, plus a summit snowfield that may require a Class 3/4 rock bypass if too steep; the primary consequence multiplier is the extreme remoteness (very long Pasayten approach, self-rescue distance) rather than technical fall exposure itself

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer route (no NWAC forecast zone specifically covers this remote Pasayten location, and the route is only climbed dry-season)

approach_variants.name: Butte Pass, Pass Butte and the connecting ridge
approach_variants.notes: Lost Peak sits several cross-country miles beyond the end of any maintained trail and is normally a three-day trip rather than a climb. The common line follows the Monument Creek trail, which is well graded and even rideable by bike for the first few miles along the creek and the Lost River, then ends abruptly at a washed-out bridge; beyond that the tread has been unmaintained for decades and is faint, brushy and choked with deadfall. Parties camp at a small pond below Butte Pass in the North Monument Creek basin. A longer line comes in from the Robinson Creek side over Shellrock Pass and is used on extended traverses. The climbing is genuinely easy; the navigation over a long ridge of false summits is not.
hazards: Loose scree on the south and southwest aspects
A long ridge of false summits, disorienting in whiteout or after dark
Cross-country travel above the passes with no trail and no cairns
Swift, cold fords of Eureka Creek and North Monument Creek during snowmelt
Afternoon thunderstorms with no shelter above treeline
Multi-day self-rescue distance from any road
approach_variants.baseFinding: The base is Butte Pass and the rise immediately above it. From the pond camp in the North Monument Creek basin, climb to the pass; the ridge running directly up out of it to Pass Butte, around 8,140 ft, is the start of the route, and Pass Butte is the first thing on the day you actually have to climb rather than walk to. Reaching its top is the confirmation, because from there the rest of the mountain lays out in front of you: a connecting ridge running southeast over a col near Point 8107 and on across a run of rises to Lost Peak. Underfoot is the second confirmation and a reassuring one, since the ridge line is mostly firm dirt and blocky talus that takes an edge, quite unlike the ball-bearing scree found on the south and southwest aspects of the peak. If the ground has gone to sliding scree you have dropped off the crest onto a flank. The real problem here is not finding the start but knowing when you have finished. The ridge throws up several rises that each look final from the one before, and nothing on it is the summit until the ground simply stops climbing to the southeast; budget for more than one disappointment and do not commit to a descent line off what you think is the top until you can see the ridge continuing no higher. Parties coming from the north sometimes traverse in across Pass Butte's slopes to stay off the loose southern aspects entirely, which is the same start by a slightly higher line.

bivy.name: Dot Lake and the Butte Pass basins — the far end of the traverse for Lost Peak
bivy.notes: LOST PEAK at 8,464 ft sits at the eastern end of this group between Monument Creek and the Lost River, and it is the awkward one — it does not fall out of a Carru and Lago camp the way those two fall out of each other. From the Shellrock country the usual line descends to Dot Lake, crosses a burned basin to Butte Pass and then works along a ridge with several false summits before the true top, which is a long day and one that parties routinely finish late. Camping at the lake rather than pushing back over Lago is what makes it sane, and it is the specific advice most trip accounts give: do not retrace the ridge, drop and camp. The alternative approach from the Monument Creek trailhead up the Lost River is a different trip entirely and its camps are covered in the Harts Pass file. Reckon on four days minimum for a party collecting Lost with the others, and note that the burn through here is extensive enough that navigation is easy and shade is nonexistent. Late July through September, and later is better for the passes.
bivy.water: Dot Lake is the dependable one and the reason to camp here rather than on the ridge. The basins beyond it toward Butte Pass are dry once the snow goes, and much of the ground between has burned, which makes the shade and the seeps both unreliable. Fill at the lake.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit, no quota. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Slate Pass, Robinson Creek or Monument Creek depending on which end you started. Camp back from the shoreline. Weed-free feed for stock, no tying animals to trees. Fires legal outside a ban but there is little to burn and the ground is fragile.
bivy.capacity: Informal ground around the lake and in the basins toward the pass, room for a party or two. Nothing developed, nothing signed, and you will almost certainly be alone.

bivy.name: The Berk Creek junction and the Middle Fork Pasayten river camps
bivy.notes: This is the hinge of the whole Middle Fork approach and it is where a party bound for MOUNT CARRU, MOUNT LAGO or LOST PEAK actually sleeps on the first night. Two roads reach it: the high start from Slate Pass at nearly 6,900 ft with a short connector down to the Middle Fork trail, or the low start from the Robinson Creek trailhead at about 2,560 ft over Robinson Pass at 6,220 ft, which is nine and a half miles before the valley walking even begins. The high start is shorter by a long way and is what most parties use. From the junction the climb to Freds Pass and the crossing of the upper Eureka Creek country puts you in position for the summits; the whole approach from a road is around fifteen miles. Being on the river rather than up at the lakes costs you height on the second day and buys you shelter, running water and a warmer night — a real trade when the high camps are exposed and dry. The forest here is patchy burn in places and blowdown varies. This is remote country by any standard and there is no mobile service anywhere in the valley.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Middle Fork Pasayten and Berk Creek meet here and both run all season. This is the last easy water before the long climb to the passes, and the country above lives on tarns and snowmelt, so fill completely.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue wilderness permit from the kiosk at Slate Pass or Robinson Creek, no quota and no reservation. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass to park. Weed-free feed for stock and no tying animals to trees overnight. Fires legal in existing rings outside a ban, though the valley is dry and bans are common by August.
bivy.capacity: A single established site at the junction where the trail up to Freds Lake and Doris Lake leaves the Middle Fork, plus scattered ground along the river flats above and below it. One or two parties each, nothing developed.

bivy.name: The high bench southwest of Shellrock Pass
bivy.notes: This is the staging camp that makes MOUNT CARRU and MOUNT LAGO short days instead of enormous ones, and it is deliberately not the same ground as the Shellrock Basin and Eureka Creek meadow camps lower down. It is a bench at around 7,500 ft immediately southwest of the pass, high enough that every summit in the group is within reach from it. For Carru the line runs west along the east fork of Eureka Creek, leaves the trail at a creek crossing and takes a red talus gully east of the Carru-Lago saddle for a few hundred feet — under two hours from camp to the 8,595 ft summit. Lago at 8,745 ft is the highest thing in this part of the wilderness and goes from the same saddle. WHAT YOU PAY FOR THE POSITION IS WATER AND WEATHER. There is no tree cover, the pass funnels wind, and a party that has not carried enough will be walking back down for it. Snow holds on the north sides of these passes into late July in an ordinary year and much later after a heavy winter, which is the real constraint on when this is worth doing. Larches turn in the last days of September and the nights at this height are properly cold by then.
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small tarn below the pass, both of them seasonal. By late summer there may be nothing at all up here and the passes on either side are reliably dry. Carry water up from the Eureka Creek meadows or the river; this is the single most common mistake made on these summits.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten permit, no quota and no reservation anywhere in this wilderness. Northwest Forest Pass to park. The bench is thin alpine ground that holds a footprint for years, so pitch on gravel or rock and leave the turf alone. Assume no fires — there is nothing to burn at this elevation and the meadows below are fragile.
bivy.capacity: Roughly half an acre of usable bench, so realistically two or three small parties. No established sites, no facilities and no shelter of any kind.

row.overview: Mount Ballard is a remote, double-summit peak sharing a long ridgeline with its higher neighbor Azurite Peak, near the head of Mill Creek and about 2 miles north of Azurite Peak. It ranks 84th on Washington's 100 highest peaks and rises about 4,000 ft above Mill Creek within roughly a mile, giving it dramatic local relief despite being a non-technical scramble. A 2023 precision survey found the true summit lies about 1,100 ft south of, and higher than, the point long mapped/benchmarked as 'Mount Ballard' (8,301 ft), which is actually a lower north sub-summit. There is no maintained trail to the top; all routes leave trail well below the summit to scramble broad talus, heather, and gully terrain.
row.beta: From Harts Pass Road, descend into the South Fork Slate Creek drainage, cross the South Fork on a metal bridge, and traverse open forest to a basin around 4,900 ft. From there climb through trees and open slopes to a bench on the east ridge (~6,200 ft), then continue up mixed class 3-4 rock and steep snow (up to 45-50°), angling left through cliff bands to reach the upper east ridge (~7,650 ft). At the col below the summit, cross a snow-covered ledge on the west face to the base of the summit gully, then scramble a short class 3-4 section, a ~10 ft class 4 corner, and blocky class 3 terrain to the true south summit. Parties describe route-finding through the cliff bands as the crux of navigation, and the final summit block as the technical crux (brief low 5th class, per one party).
row.turnaround: There is no fixed clock-time turnaround — the approach is long (documented round trips of 8.5-10 hours) and includes route-finding through cliff bands and steep snow. Set a turnaround based on remaining daylight, weather trends, and snow condition: wet, sun-softened snow on the 45-50° slopes sharply increases fall risk, and if the col/summit gully hasn't been reached with enough daylight and stable snow remaining to retrace the route, retreat.
row.face: East Ridge (Slate Creek approach) with a West Face finish to the true summit
row.permit: No wilderness permit applies - Mount Ballard is on Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest land and is not within the Pasayten Wilderness. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at some trailheads.
row.descent: Descend the same broad south-facing slopes/gully used on the ascent back down to the basin above the Azurite Mine (~6,600 ft); the scree and talus are loose, so downclimb carefully and avoid being directly above other climbers to prevent knocking rock onto them. From the basin, reverse whichever approach was used (Mill Creek Trail, or Mill Creek plus West Fork Methow River Trail/PCT) back to the trailhead — the lower, brush-choked stretch of the Mill Creek Trail is typically as slow going out as coming in.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek ford
waypoints.note: Ford Mill Creek just below the trail junction — last reliable, easy-to-reach water before the long climb toward Azurite.

waypoints.name: Mill Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Canyon Creek tread here and turn up the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail; maintained trail effectively ends beyond this point.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Mill Creek Trail
waypoints.note: Tread disappears under heavy slide alder and downed timber left from the mine-era trail's disuse — expect a slow, scratchy alder-hacking bushwhack for several miles.

waypoints.name: Azurite Mine
waypoints.note: Flat ground amid the old defunct copper/silver mine workings on Mill Creek; the common overnight camp before pushing toward the Ballard basin.

waypoints.name: Azurite–Ballard basin
waypoints.note: Reached via roughly 3 more brush-choked miles above the mine; open basin at the base of Ballard's south slopes and a typical bivy before the summit push.

waypoints.name: South-face brush and gully route-finding
waypoints.note: Steep, loose terrain with several look-alike chutes low on the south face — picking the wrong gully here is the main way parties get cliffed out or turned back.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large parking lot on SR 20 just east of milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass. The trail follows Canyon Creek about 6 miles to the Mill Creek Trail junction, the start of this route's approach. The east-side line up the East Ridge starts elsewhere, at a locked gate on the Slate Creek road below Harts Pass (about 3,800 ft).

row.detailed_rack: No technical rock rack is needed for the standard route. Bring an ice axe and crampons for the steep (up to 45-50°) snowfields below the col, which can persist well into summer. A single short rope with a few slings can be carried to protect the brief low 5th-class/exposed class 4 step near the true summit for less experienced or larger parties, though most parties free-solo it.
pro_tips: Combine with Azurite from a shared high camp
Stay on firmer rock to avoid loose scree near the top
row.pro_needs: No fixed protection (bolts or pitons) exists on the route — it's a scramble with one short, exposed low-5th-class move near the summit. Any belay on that step would be improvised off natural rock features.
row.approach: Standard approach: drive Highway 20 to the Canyon Creek Trailhead near milepost 141, west of Rainy Pass and follow the Mill Creek/Azurite Pass Trail (#755) up Canyon Creek then Mill Creek — about 11 miles (roughly 6 along Canyon Creek, then 5 up Mill Creek) to the site of the defunct Azurite Mine, then a further ~3 increasingly faint, brush-choked miles (slide alder and downed timber are common since the trail has seen little maintenance since the mine closed) to roughly the 14-mile mark, where a boot path continues about 1.5 more miles to Azurite Pass (6,680+ ft). A longer alternate, more often used for combined Azurite-Ballard trips, starts at the West Fork Methow River Trailhead (#480) near River Bend Campground: follow that trail ~8 miles to the PCT, then the PCT south ~1.5 miles to Horse Heaven Camp before joining the Mill Creek Trail to the pass — this option runs closer to 25 miles round trip with about 6,000 ft of elevation gain.
row.descent_text: Descend the south slopes, retracing the ascent into the basin.
row.bail: Reverse the scramble; no fixed anchors required.

pitch_detail.notes: Old road/forest traverse from Slate Creek Road gate, over the South Fork bridge, to the ~4,900 ft basin.
Ascend snow/rock from the 4,900 ft basin to a 6,200 ft bench, then continue to ~7,650 ft, angling left through cliff bands; slopes up to 45-50°.
Traverse a snow-covered ledge on the west face to the summit gully; finish with a ~10 ft class 4 corner and short class 3 blocks to the true (south) summit.

itinerary.cal: The Mill Creek Trail is severely brushed-in and essentially unmaintained year-round, so most parties wait until after peak snowmelt (mid-July through September) to reduce stream crossings and lingering snow on the upper mountain.

days.note: Hike the Canyon Creek Trail (about 6 good miles) then turn onto the Mill Creek Trail (about 5 miles). Parties describe Mill Creek as badly overgrown and blown-down — the first 4 brushy miles alone can eat 4 hours — so budget a long day even though the mileage looks modest. Camp near the Azurite Mine site at Ballard's base.

days.note: A steep, mostly off-trail scramble on brush, scree, and rock with two well-known cruxes: thick brush low on the mountain, and route-finding into the correct summit gully higher up (sustained 3rd class with a couple of exposed 4th class steps). Parties commonly tack on nearby Azurite Peak from the same camp if time and weather allow, but Ballard alone is already a long day — parties note a long evening getting back to camp.

access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: No climbing or wilderness permit required for day climbing. Dispersed camping capped at 10 days; no campfires at dispersed sites; bear-resistant food storage required; dogs on leash ≤6 ft.
access.permit: No wilderness permit currently required (route lies just outside the Pasayten Wilderness boundary).
access.closures: Harts Pass Road (FR-5400) closed to wheeled vehicles Dec 1 through spring snowmelt; check current Forest Service alerts, as storm damage (e.g. rockfall, washouts) has caused additional out-of-season closures in some years
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District. The peak sits just outside the formal Pasayten Wilderness boundary (like neighboring Azurite Peak), so wilderness-specific rules do not apply here.

climate.fall: An October ascent found fresh snow above roughly 7,000 ft with the lower approach snow-free; early winter storms can arrive by mid-October.
climate.spring: Significant snowpack lingers on the upper mountain; a late-May ascent found ~2 ft of snow at Harts Pass and wet, unstable snow on the route.
climate.summer: Best window for the class 3-4 rock, typically July-September, though shaded gullies and the col area can hold snow well into summer.
climate.winter: Harts Pass Road closed; deep snowpack and avalanche terrain make winter ascent a different, far more serious undertaking.
climate.typical: Short climbing window: summer days are typically dry and warm with a real risk of afternoon thunderstorms building over the North Cascades crest. Snow can linger in north-facing gullies and along the approach into July. Access is effectively blocked by snow and high, unbridged creek crossings from roughly October through June.

emergency.notes: Very remote; cell coverage is unreliable in the Canyon Creek and Mill Creek drainages. Vehicle access is from SR 20 (or Harts Pass Road for the Slate Creek side), and any rescue response will be lengthy given driving time plus the multi-hour approach.
emergency.rangerStation: Methow Valley Ranger District, 24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA 98862, (509) 996-4000
