approach_variants.name: Mill Creek and the Azurite Pass side
approach_variants.notes: This is the approach the peak is normally catalogued under and the one that pairs naturally with Azurite. It runs from Highway 20 up Canyon Creek and then Mill Creek on tread that has seen little maintenance since the mine closed, where slide alder and downed timber are the recurring complaint and parties routinely lose the path entirely for stretches. A longer alternative from the West Fork Methow trailhead reaches the same country by way of the Pacific Crest Trail and Horse Heaven Camp and is often preferred for combined trips despite the extra mileage. Camp is usually made near the old mine or in the basin above it. Note that the point long marked on maps as Mount Ballard is a lower north sub-summit; the true high point lies about 1,100 ft further south and is slightly higher.
hazards: Slide alder and downed timber on an unmaintained approach trail
Route-finding through brush pockets and broken gullies on the flank
Loose, rotten rock and exposure near the summit ridge
Snowfields into July that can require an ice axe
Open upper mountain with full lightning exposure
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: On this side the walking ends at the old Azurite Mine site around 5,900 ft and the brush begins immediately. The base of the climb is the open basin at roughly 6,600 ft above and east of the mine, sitting between Ballard and the ridge running out toward Azurite. You know you are in it when the timber gives out and you can see the peak's flank in one piece above you rather than through trees. That flank is the difficulty: it is not a single clean face but a patchwork of brush pockets, rock ribs and short gullies, and parties consistently find that the hard part of the day is not the scrambling but picking which gully continues, a decision that comes to a head around 7,400 ft. Read the ground rather than committing early, because a gully that closes out costs a long reversal. The obvious-looking answer is a trap: the south ridge presents as a clean continuous line from below and is blocked higher by a notch with a gendarme in it, so a party that racks up the ridge crest on sight will be turned around. The other check is on which summit you are heading for. There are two high points on this mountain, and the northern one, the one carrying the old survey mark, is the lower; keep working south along the crest until the ground stops rising. If you find yourself on the connecting ridge with Azurite you have gone north and are on the wrong end of the massif.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Slate Creek and the east ridge
approach_variants.notes: The other side of the mountain, approached from the Slate Creek road system rather than from Mill Creek, and the line most parties who climb this peak actually use. It is shorter, the forest below camp is comparatively brush-free, and the route-finding above camp is far more legible than on the Mill Creek side, at the cost of one genuinely steep step low down and some exposed ledge work near the top. Snow conditions change this route's character completely: a filled-in slot low down and firm snow in the upper cirque make for fast travel, while dry late-season conditions leave loose rock and slippery vegetation. Camp is normally made in a scree basin below the east ridge.
hazards: A steep vegetated step through the lowest cliff band, the hardest ground on the route
Exposed ledge traverse above the high saddle
Loose rock in the summit gully with a party stacked below
Steep snow in the east cirque into midsummer
Full lightning exposure on the open upper mountain
Very remote, with a long and difficult evacuation if injured
approach_variants.baseFinding: The approach has one unmistakable marker and the climb has another. Start at the locked gate on the Slate Creek road at about 3,800 ft and walk the South Fork road for roughly a mile and a half to an old vehicle bridge at about 4,000 ft; that bridge is the single positive check on the whole road walk, and if you have not crossed it you are still on the main branch. From the bridge, head south through open, brush-free forest for another mile and a half or so to a scree basin around 4,800 ft, the usual camp. From camp the route climbs through tight forest and then open scree to a shoulder on the east ridge at roughly 6,200 ft. The base of the real climbing is right there and it is easy to identify because it is the wrong colour: a steep slot of heather and grass cutting through the lowest cliff band, green vegetation in an otherwise rocky wall, and the only weakness in that band. It is the steepest ground on the route and it is the crux. Bare rock gullies to either side look more like a climb and are harder and looser, so the vegetated slot is the line. Above it stay on the rib and follow the ridge crest, then the scree slope and east cirque, to a high saddle north of the summit. From that saddle do not go straight up; traverse ledges, some of them exposed, to a narrow gully that gains the summit block.

climbing_route.label: South slopes and gullies from the Mill Creek basin
climbing_route.notes: From the basin above the old Azurite Mine (about 6,600 ft), leave the trail and scramble north up Ballard's broad south-facing slopes and gullies, watching for the correct gully to the true summit block.

bivy.name: Canyon Creek trailhead, SR 20
bivy.notes: This is the western door to Azurite and Ballard, and the drive alone puts it a long way from anywhere — roughly thirty-three miles east of Marblemount and sixteen west of Rainy Pass, with no services in either direction. Parties commonly sleep in the lot before starting, and the low elevation means it is warm and buggy in early summer when the peaks above are still white. The trail from here runs about six miles up Canyon Creek before the Mill Creek trail branches right at around two thousand eight hundred feet, a third of a mile past the trail's own crossing of Mill Creek. The whole point of understanding this trailhead is the arithmetic that follows: the pass is around six thousand seven hundred feet and the car is at nineteen hundred, so this is a genuine multi-day trip with more than four thousand seven hundred feet of gain before any climbing starts. Access depends entirely on the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts this stretch of highway from late November or early December until somewhere between mid April and early May, occasionally much later after a damaging winter.
bivy.water: No potable water at the trailhead. Canyon Creek is close by and needs filtering.
bivy.permit: No camping permit. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park. This is national forest and there is no quota or reservation of any kind. A separate trail from this same lot runs north into the Pasayten Wilderness, which does carry a free self-issue permit from the kiosk, so read the board and take one only if your route actually crosses that boundary.
bivy.capacity: A large parking area just east of milepost 141, roughly a third of the way between Newhalem and Rainy Pass. Rarely busy, because almost nobody uses the trail these peaks need.

name: Kautz Glacier
prior_findings: 'Kautz Headwall' names both the Kautz route's ice chute and a separate ski line; decide which this row is. Kautz chute/headwall lengths vary by year; state them as a seasonal range if two sources support it.

earlier_research.evidence: The waypoint now reads 10,800 (already resolved), but approach_variants still said 11,000-11,100 ft. The park route brief puts today's Camp Hazard at 10,800 ft (the original, unused site nearer 11,000 ft); a trip report also reached Camp Hazard at about 10,800 ft.

The park route brief: the gully is climbed from 6,800 ft where the Wilson meets the Nisqually to the large bench at 7,300 ft. The waypoint's own directions, the approach, approach_variants and pitch_detail all agree on 6,800-7,400 ft; 8,800 is the lone outlier. Pin set to the bench at the gully top (7,300 ft).

earlier_research.correct_value: 60 m rope per rope team
earlier_research.evidence: gear, rappels, rappel_count_note and descent_text all assume a single 60 m rope; a trip report on the route carried a 60 m rope for a three-person team. No source recommends 30-40 m.

earlier_research.correct_value: west (climber's-left) side
earlier_research.evidence: The park route brief: the centre and climber's right (east) side of the Turtle is threatened by icefall, so stay on the west side near the rock ridge; it also puts Camp Hazard on the climber's left of the snowfield. Heading uphill (north), west is climber's left; the approach and waypoint already say so.

earlier_research.correct_value: Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista / Nisqually Moraine, cross the Nisqually Glacier, up Wapowety Cleaver to Camp Hazard
earlier_research.evidence: The park route brief: the Paradise approach follows the Skyline Trail and Nisqually Moraine Trail, drops onto and crosses the Nisqually Glacier, then climbs to the Castle and Camp Hazard. A trip report describes the same line: Paradise to Glacier Vista, down 400 ft to the Nisqually, across to the Fan and up. Neither goes up the Muir Snowfield. Fixed in itinerary day 1 and the matching timing section note.

earlier_research.correct_value: Upper step AI3 (the crux); lower step easier
earlier_research.evidence: The park route brief states "the technical grade of AI3" and calls the upper step up to over 300 ft of AI3; it does not rate it only AI2 and short. A trip report also grades the route "III, AI2-3" and another describes two AI3 steps. The gear line (which also named a source) was the error; grade, ice_grade and pitch_detail stand.

Sources disagree and vary by year: the park brief gives a lower step from a short pitch to ~250 ft and an upper step from a short pitch to 300+ ft; one route page describes two ~400 ft pitches at 35-40 and 45-50 degrees; a trip report gives a first step to 50 degrees under a pitch and a second to 60 degrees a bit over a pitch; the 2020 ranger update calls the main ice 300 ft in two 60 m pitches. No two sources agree on one set of lengths.

earlier_research.correct_value: III
earlier_research.evidence: grade and commitment say III; a trip report grades the route "Grade: III, AI2-3", and two others call it "Grade II or III" / "II-III". No source found gives Grade IV, so the III-IV alpine_grade is the outlier.

The park brief gives only 1.8-2 miles to the Nisqually and 11-12 mi for the whole route; no source states the Paradise-to-Camp Hazard mileage, so neither 5 nor 7 can be confirmed. The waypoint order (0, 1.5, 3.5, 7, 13) is monotonic, so it is not nulled.

Retry found only more year-dependent figures: a 2024 park conditions report describes a short mandatory lower step (~50 ft) climbed in several pitches in that season; another party reports about two full 60 m pitches of AI2; a climber's inclinometer read 35 degrees overall and 42-44 at the steepest. No two independent sources give one set of step lengths; the chute's size changes year to year. Settling it needs an owner decision to state the chute as a seasonal range (e.g. the park's 'short pitch to 250 ft / short pitch to 300+ ft') in every field, rather than a single figure.

New sources give only whole-route figures: a guide service states ~10 miles Paradise to summit; a 2020 carry-over trip logged 18.5 miles total up the Kautz and down the DC. No source states the Paradise-to-Camp Hazard mileage, so neither 5 nor 7 can be confirmed. A GPS track of the Paradise-Camp Hazard leg from two parties would settle it.

Timing and itinerary give 12 h; partner requirements say ~17 h. The NPS Kautz route brief gives no summit-day duration, and trip reports vary widely (3h45 to ~9 h camp-to-rim alone, plus a variable DC descent). No two sources state a car-to-car summit-day figure; a published camp-to-Paradise time from two sources would settle it.

Timing/itinerary say 6 h; partner requirements say 7-9 h. The NPS brief describes the Castle (9,200-9,500 ft) as the usual camp for 2-3 night trips and Camp Hazard for single-night pushes but states no hours; no two sources give a Paradise-to-Camp-Hazard time.

Rack says 4-6 per rope team, the summit waypoint says 6-8. The NPS brief lists 2-4 ice screws PER PERSON (which for a 2-3 person team spans both figures), and the row's own gear list notes counts vary with ice coverage. No two sources give a per-rope-team count.

row.fa: Hans Fuhrer, Heinie Fuhrer, Roger Toll, and Harry Myers, June 26-28, 1920 (August Kautz's 1857 party reached ~12,000 ft on this line)
row.season: Mid-May through early August; use drops sharply after August 1 as the approach and glaciers deteriorate
gear: Standard glacier travel kit: harness, crevasse-rescue gear (prussiks/ascenders)
60 m rope per rope team
A few ice screws and 1-2 pickets per rope team for the chute — parties have carried anything from 8 screws and 2 pickets to screws they never placed, so exact counts track current ice coverage
A second tool — useful specifically in the ice chute, whose upper step is the route's AI3 crux
Crampons
Helmet — rockfall risk noted on the route
hazards: The Kautz ice chute — firm alpine ice, usually one to two short steep pitches that can be bare and hard late season
Rock and icefall off the Kautz headwall and Wapowety Cleaver, worst once the sun hits
Crevasse navigation on the upper Nisqually and Kautz glaciers
Year-to-year variability: in lean years the ice steepens and lengthens
Moat/bergschrund at the base of the Kautz Ice Chute where it meets the glacier below — check current condition before committing.
row.overview: The Kautz Glacier is Rainier's classic intermediate route — a step up from the standard glacier slogs, with one or two genuine pitches of alpine ice in the Kautz ice chute. It climbs the south side from Paradise via the Nisqually Glacier and Wapowety Cleaver area to a high camp around Camp Hazard, then takes the ice chute and upper Kautz Glacier to the summit. It's the natural first 'real' alpine route for climbers who have done the DC and want ice.
row.beta: No guide-maintained trail or fixed protection; requires proficiency in ice climbing, short-pitching, and crevasse rescue. The technical ice pitches occur near 12,000 ft, adding fatigue to the difficulty.
row.turnaround: Plan to be at the top of the chute well before midday; if the ice is taking too long, retreat down-climbing/rappelling before afternoon warming.
row.rappels: 2-5 rappels through the Kautz ice chute, depending on conditions and how much rope you carry: 1-3 down the upper ice step and 1-2 down the lower one, all on V-thread anchors you thread yourself. The four stations listed here are a representative middle count for a party on a single 60 m rope - fewer with two ropes, more if short-pitching.
row.face: South side, Kautz Glacier / Wapowety Cleaver
row.permit: Mount Rainier: climbing on glaciers or above 10,000 ft requires the park's climbing registration; overnight high camps also need a wilderness permit.
row.comms: Cell reception available at most locations above ~6,000 ft.
row.descent: Descend via Kautz Glacier and Wilson Glacier to Nisqually Glacier area, then descend Nisqually to Paradise. This descent is exposed and requires careful snow bridge evaluation; late-season descents on Nisqually are dangerous due to crevasse widening. Alternatively, descend via Disappointment Cleaver to Camp Muir.
obj_haz: Ice/serac fall from Kautz Ice Cliff
Crevasses and hidden bridges on glaciers
Steep ice and mixed terrain (45-50 degrees)

waypoints.name: Glacier Vista
waypoints.directions: Leave the upper Paradise lot on the Skyline Trail and follow the standard Muir-bound tread as it climbs above the meadows. Glacier Vista is the marked overlook where the Nisqually opens up several hundred feet below you. This is where the Kautz route leaves the trail system for good.

waypoints.name: Wilson Gully (Crux)
waypoints.directions: Follow the climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, then drop onto the Nisqually and rope up before starting across — the crossing threads crevassed terrain under icefall and is genuinely dangerous in poor visibility. Take the line of least resistance over to the far side and the distinct low-angle snow gully there, then climb it to the bench above at roughly 7,300 to 7,400 ft. Move through this stretch early and do not stop in it.

waypoints.name: Camp Hazard
waypoints.directions: From the top of the gully follow the ridge line up past the string of established camps — Wilson Moraine, then Lower and Upper Castle, which is where most parties spend the first night and where running water is usually available from mid-June on. Above the Castle the Turtle snowfield leads to Camp Hazard: sun-cupped firm snow and glacier ice, so keep an ice tool in hand. Stay to the west side of the snowfield, because its centre and east flank are raked by rock and ice off the Kautz Ice Cliff.

waypoints.name: Columbia Crest
waypoints.directions: Leave camp in the dark. Drop a couple of hundred feet through the gully between the rock cliff and the ice cliff, then move left around the base of the ice cliff to the foot of the chute — this is the deposition zone under the ice cliff and the reason for the alpine start, so cross it moving. The chute is two or three pitches of roughly 40 to 50 degree snow and ice, bare and hard in a lean year, and six to eight screws is a sensible rack. Above it, angle up the upper Kautz and Wapowety Cleaver, working around crevasses, moats along the rock, and a large bergschrund near the crater rim before the flat walk to the top.

row.detailed_rack: Per person: ice axe plus a second technical tool, 12-point crampons, helmet, harness. Per rope team: 60 m rope, 4–6 ice screws (for the chute), 2–4 pickets, crevasse-rescue kit, a couple of slings/cordelettes for V-thread or picket anchors.

Bring enough screws to protect the steepest step and build a rappel anchor

row.watch_out:
Crevasse danger in high sections: endless bottom crevasse in snowfield near top
Serac exposure on upper terrain above 11,000 ft
Two significant ice pitches (35-40 and 45-50 degrees) requiring ice tools and protection
Fixed rappel line may or may not be present at drainage gully - verify current conditions
Snow bridge hazards documented in lower snowfield
Route-finding precision critical at lower elevations to locate snow/ice ramp
row.pro_needs: Mixed glacier + ice protection: screws for the ice steps, pickets for snow, plus standard crevasse-rescue gear. No rock pro needed.
row.best_season: May through mid-July, before the chute bares out to hard ice and rockfall increases. Early season offers the most forgiving snow-over-ice.
row.approach: Two approaches are used, both arduous. The Paradise approach (5,420 ft) follows the Skyline Trail to the Nisqually Moraine Trail, then a climbers' path along the moraine to about 6,300 ft, where several boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier itself; most parties rope up here, since the crossing threads through heavily crevassed terrain exposed to icefall from above and is genuinely dangerous in reduced visibility. From the glacier's east moraine there are two ways up onto Wapowety Cleaver: a flat traverse to the base of 'The Fan,' a gully with avalanche, rockfall, and steep-slope hazard, climbed directly to a bench at 7,300 ft; or a climb up the Nisqually/Wilson Glacier margin at 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft 'Wilson Bench.' From the bench, snow slopes lead to the ridge crest and a string of established camps at increasing elevation — Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft), and the Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft, the most common base for a summit push, with running water from mid-June on). The alternative Van Trump Park approach starts at the Comet Falls Trailhead (3,650 ft): follow the maintained Comet Falls Trail 2.2 miles (2,000 ft gain) to a junction, continue toward Van Trump Park another 0.6 miles to where maintained trail ends, then follow unmaintained social trails up a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, followed up to the Upper Castle (9,500 ft) where the two approaches merge — descending this line requires a saved GPS track to relocate the correct moraine and treeline trail junction, even in good visibility, per NPS guidance. Above the Castle, the Turtle Snowfield (slopes up to 45°) is climbed on its west (climber's-left) side, close to the rock ridge, since its center and climber's-right (east) side are threatened by ice and rockfall from above. Established high camps continue at Camp Hazard (10,800 ft, on the climber's-left side at the top of the Turtle Snowfield), the Rock Step camps (11,250 ft), and exposed Wapowety Cleaver bivy sites (13,100 ft, used mainly by parties planning to descend via the Disappointment Cleaver rather than reverse the Kautz).
row.descent_text: Descending the Kautz is a real technical descent, not a walk-off, and involves multiple rappels through the ice chute — typically two to five depending on conditions, ice quality, and rope length. From the top of Wapowety Cleaver, parties reverse the glacier line down through crevassed terrain to the top of the ice chute, then find easier ground to climber's-left/east to belay into the chute rather than committing to team-arrest on exposed ice. The upper ice step (commonly a short pitch up to 300+ ft of AI3 alpine ice) is rappelled: the NPS route brief states this takes anywhere from one to three rappels depending on rope length and how many ropes the team carries, using 'Zero-Thread' ice anchors — a variant of the V-thread/Abalakov anchor chosen because it's equally strong but leaves no gear behind; there is no fixed/bolted hardware on this route, and the Park Service explicitly discourages leaving V-thread anchors in place between ascent and descent since they can melt out. Below the upper step, lower-angle snow leads to the lower ice step, typically descended with one to two more rappels on the same anchor style — so two to five rappels total through the chute is realistic for most parties on a single 60m rope, fewer with two ropes or more if short-pitching. After the chute, a fast, alert traverse back toward the Rock Step is required, since this stretch sits directly under the active Kautz Ice Cliff. Climbing back up through the Rock Step itself (awkward 5th-class moves protected by fixed rope and old slings on rock anchors) returns parties to high camp; from there it's a walk/glissade down the Turtle Snowfield, back across the Nisqually or Wilson glacier crossing, and out to Paradise (or back down through Van Trump Park). A significant number of teams instead choose the 'up-and-over' option — descending the easier, non-technical Disappointment Cleaver/Muir Snowfield line from the summit to Camp Muir and Paradise — specifically to avoid re-descending the ice chute and Rock Step on tired legs, at the cost of having to haul full camping gear over the summit.
row.bail: From the ice chute you can rappel/down-climb back to Camp Hazard. Camp Hazard / the Castle is the high-camp bail point; below that, retreat across the lower glaciers toward Paradise. The DC descent is the standard 'escape' once on the summit.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the heavily crevassed Nisqually Glacier roped (about 6,300 ft), climb the Fan or the Wilson gully to the bench at 7,300–7,400 ft, then follow snow up Wapowety Cleaver past the Castle camps (9,200–9,500 ft). The Turtle Snowfield reaches 45°; keep to its west side by the rock ridge, since the centre and east are raked by ice and rockfall. Camp Hazard sits at 10,800 ft.

From the top bivy sites a climbers' trail leads up and left to a notch on the ridge (about 11,000–11,250 ft) with a fixed rope on rock anchors. The short, technical rock step directly below it is down-climbed on belay using the rope, or rappelled, onto the Kautz Glacier. Early season it may be buried in snow. Coming back up it is awkward 5th-class moves on old slings and fixed line.

From the base of the step, traverse onto the Kautz Glacier and into the ice chute directly beneath the Kautz Ice Cliff. This is a very active zone littered with ice and rock debris of every size: do not stop, regroup, or take breaks here. Move through it quickly and watch above. The same traverse must be crossed again on the way back to the Rock Step.

The first and easier step: anything from a short pitch of steep snow to about 250 ft of alpine ice depending on season, with narrow crevasses sometimes crossing the slope. Later in summer water runs over it, so place screws out of the flow. Most parties pitch it or short-pitch it; on descent it takes one or two rappels on ice threads.

Between the steps the chute is snow-covered all year, anywhere from firm névé to slushy sun cups, over roughly 200–400 vertical ft. Most parties simul-climb or short-rope it. It is generally free of crevasses but exposed to ice and rock knocked down from above, especially by parties climbing overhead, so do not linger below others.

The technical crux: from a short pitch to more than 300 ft of sustained AI3 near 12,000 ft. Most parties take the centre; late season, penitentes on the climber's right go easier. Night brings brittle refrozen ice, daytime a slushy skin; clear the surface for screws. Alpine ice breaks off in plates, so belay out of the leader's fall line. Descend by one to three rappels on ice threads.

Regroup near 12,000 ft and rope for glacier travel; the next 1,000 ft are mellow but hold some of the mountain's biggest, bell-shaped crevasses, so probe every bridge. Trend up and right to Wapowety Cleaver near 13,000 ft, watching for moats. Onto the Nisqually, work east to about 13,500 ft, then west to the saddle with Point Success; just under 500 ft more past the bergschrund reaches the crater rim.

access.fees: $82 per person per climb - Climbing Cost Recovery Fee (2026 rate). It is charged per climb, not per season. Separate from the park entrance fee.
access.notes: How to get it: pay online in advance (pay.gov / recreation.gov), then register in person. Winter (Sept 16–May 21): self-issue at the Paradise Old Station kiosk after paying online. Summer (May 22–Sept 30): no self-issue — register at a Wilderness Information Center (Longmire, Paradise, or White River); roughly half of summer registration slots are held for walk-up, up to 24 hrs ahead. No timed-entry vehicle reservation is in effect for the 2026 season, so park entry itself is first-come, first-served.
access.rules: Blue bags required for human waste above high camp — pack out and deposit only in barrels marked "Human Waste" at Camp Muir or the trailhead; do not cache on-route. Check-out is required after every climb.
access.parking_pass: Not a Northwest Forest Pass (that's a USFS pass and doesn't apply inside the park). Standard NPS entrance fee applies: $30/vehicle (7 consecutive days), $55 Mount Rainier annual pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.

approach_variants.name: Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson bench
approach_variants.notes:
From Paradise (5,420 ft) follow the paved trail about a mile to Glacier Vista, then the Nisqually Moraine climbers' path to roughly 6,300 ft where boot paths drop onto the Nisqually Glacier. Rope up here — the crossing is through crevassed ground exposed to icefall from above and is dangerous in poor visibility.

From the east side of the glacier there are two ways onto the Wapowety Cleaver ground. One is a flat traverse to the base of a gully known as The Fan, climbed directly to a bench at about 7,300 ft; The Fan carries avalanche, rockfall and steep-snow hazard. The other climbs the Nisqually/Wilson margin at about 6,800 ft through an often-crevassed gully to the same 7,300–7,400 ft bench.

Above the bench, snow slopes lead to a string of established camps: Wilson Moraine (8,200–8,600 ft), Lower Castle (9,250 ft) and Upper Castle (9,400–9,500 ft), the most common base, with running water from about mid-June. Higher again, rock islands along the west edge of the Turtle snowfield between roughly 9,500 and 10,500 ft hold good bivouacs, and there is usually flowing water at the snowfield edges in warm weather.

Camp Hazard (about 10,800 ft) is the traditional high camp and is named for what sits above it: the Kautz Ice Cliff. Many parties deliberately camp lower and climb through Camp Hazard early rather than sleep under the cliff. On the Turtle, keep to the western, climber's-left side — the centre and east are raked by ice and rock off the cliff.

Rainier permits apply: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, and a wilderness permit for each overnight camp in the high-use season.
approach_variants.season: Mid-May into early August; the approach and glaciers deteriorate quickly after that
hazards: Serac fall from the Kautz Ice Cliff onto Camp Hazard and the traverse beneath it
Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing
Avalanche, rockfall and steep snow in The Fan gully
Ice and rockfall raking the centre and east side of the Turtle snowfield
Thin or rotten ice in the chute late in the season
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The single most useful fact about this route is that the technical climbing starts BELOW Camp Hazard, not above it. Parties who expect to walk out of camp and start climbing walk straight under the ice cliff.

From camp, pick up the climbers' path on the rock and follow it to a short rappel, which often has a fixed line on it. That rappel is the confirmation you are on the right line — it drops you about 150 ft into the drainage gully at the bottom of the ice cliff. You should be LOSING height before you gain any.

From the bottom of that gully, traverse west, underneath the ice cliff, until you can see an obvious snow-and-ice ramp running up on your left. That ramp is the Kautz ice chute, and it is the start of the route. The older description of the same ground is: down over the ridge, down the gully about 150 ft, then either cross the icefall into the broad chute or continue down and around the toe of the icefall to reach the bottom of the chute.

What you should find in the chute: a first pitch of roughly 400 ft at 35–40 degrees on stepped ground that most parties climb with a single tool, then a second pitch of roughly 400 ft at 45–50 degrees where a second tool earns its place. In lean years the ice can be thin, rotten or frozen dirt rather than good ice; the angle, not the quality, is what identifies it.

Negative marker: if you are climbing directly up from Camp Hazard toward the ice cliff, stop. That is the serac fall line, and it is the reason the camp has its name.

approach_variants.name: Comet Falls and Van Trump Park
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Comet Falls trailhead (3,650 ft) on the Longmire–Paradise road. The maintained Comet Falls Trail climbs 2.2 miles and about 2,000 ft to a junction, then continues toward Van Trump Park for another 0.6 miles to the end of maintained tread. From there unmaintained social trails climb a steep moraine crest to about 6,500 ft and onto the permanent snow of the Van Trump Glacier remnant, which is followed to the Upper Castle at roughly 9,500 ft where this approach merges with the Paradise line.

The advantage is that it never crosses the Nisqually Glacier. The cost is a lower start, a steeper carry and a descent that is genuinely hard to reverse: the Park Service's own advice is to save a GPS track, because relocating the correct moraine and the treeline trail junction on the way down is difficult even in clear weather. Several parties a season lose that junction and end up bushwhacking.
approach_variants.season: Same window; avoids the Nisqually Glacier crossing entirely
hazards: Losing the moraine crest and the treeline trail junction on descent — carry a saved track
Steep unmaintained moraine travel above the end of maintained trail
Same serac and ice-cliff exposure above the Castle and at Camp Hazard
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variant's finding problem is the reverse of most: the hard recognition is on the way down, not the way up. On the way up, the sequence is trail to a junction, more trail to the end of maintained tread, then a steep moraine crest — if you are still on graded tread above about 6,500 ft you have followed the wrong branch toward Van Trump Park's meadows rather than the climbers' line.

The merge point is the Upper Castle at about 9,400–9,500 ft, a rock rib with established camp sites and, from mid-June, running water. Once you are there the route ahead is the same as the Paradise approach: up the Turtle keeping to its western edge, to Camp Hazard, and then DOWN a short rappel into the gully beneath the ice cliff to reach the chute.

bivy.name: Camp Hazard
bivy.notes: On the climber's left of the Turtle Snowfield at about 10,800 ft: three large rock rings below the Kautz Ice Cliff, and the highest regular camp on the route. It shortens summit day. The original Camp Hazard, nearer 11,000 ft, sits in the fall line of ice from the cliff and is not used.

bivy.name: Castle camps on Wapowety Cleaver
bivy.notes: Two camp areas on the ridge below Wapowety Cleaver at the edge of the Wilson Glacier. Lower Castle, about 9,250 ft, has a few closely spaced rock rings for small parties; Upper Castle, 9,400 to 9,500 ft, has large rock rings and is where most parties camp. Wind-exposed.
